outputs.L3:
This paper examines the role of transition-metal elements in determining the electronic structure of quasicrystals and related complex phases. In particular, it considers how the presence of these elements affects the formation of characteristic electronic states and contributes to the distinctive physical behavior observed in such materials.

The paper also discusses the influence of transition-metal elements on transport properties, including their impact on electrical conduction. Since quasicrystals and related complex phases often display unusual transport behavior, understanding the contribution of transition-metal atoms is essential for clarifying the relationship between atomic structure, electronic states, and macroscopic properties.

Rather than presenting an exhaustive review, the work is intended as a brief overview of the subject. It highlights selected aspects of the problem and summarizes key ideas concerning the connection between transition-metal chemistry, electronic structure, and transport phenomena in complex metallic phases.

Several parts of the research described in the paper were carried out or initiated in collaboration with Professor T. Fujiwara. His contributions helped shape important aspects of the work and provided valuable insight into the electronic properties of quasicrystals and related materials.
outputs.L4:
This paper discusses the role of transition-metal elements in determining the electronic structure and transport properties of quasicrystals and related complex metallic phases. Quasicrystals, with their long-range quasiperiodic order and lack of conventional translational symmetry, exhibit electronic and transport behavior that differs markedly from that of ordinary crystalline metals. These unusual properties are closely connected not only with their complex atomic arrangements, but also with the chemical nature of their constituent elements. Among these, transition metals play a particularly important role.

The discussion is based in part on research carried out or initiated in collaboration with Prof. T. Fujiwara, whose work made significant contributions to the understanding of electronic states in quasicrystalline and approximant systems. A central theme is that transition-metal atoms strongly affect the electronic density of states near the Fermi level through their localized d orbitals and their hybridization with the sp states of other constituent elements. This hybridization can lead to the formation of a pseudogap, a characteristic reduction in the electronic density of states around the Fermi energy, which is often associated with the stability of many quasicrystals and complex alloy phases.

The presence of transition metals also has important consequences for transport properties. Because of the complex atomic structure and the particular electronic states produced by transition-metal hybridization, electrons in these materials may show reduced mobility, unusual temperature dependence of conductivity, and behavior that cannot be explained by simple free-electron models. In many cases, the electronic states are neither fully extended as in ordinary metals nor fully localized as in insulators, but display intermediate or critical character. Such features are essential for interpreting the anomalous electrical conductivity observed in quasicrystals and related approximant crystals.

By examining these effects, the paper emphasizes that transition metals are not merely additional chemical components, but key elements that shape the fundamental physical properties of complex metallic systems. Their d-electron states, bonding characteristics, and interaction with the quasiperiodic or highly complex lattice structure are crucial for understanding why these materials differ from conventional metals and alloys. The study of transition-metal-containing quasicrystals therefore provides valuable insight into the broader relationship between atomic structure, electronic states, phase stability, and transport phenomena in complex metallic matter.

Overall, the paper highlights the significance of transition metals in the physics of quasicrystals and related phases. It shows that a proper understanding of these materials requires careful consideration of both their structural complexity and their transition-metal electronic character. In doing so, it also reflects the continuing influence of Prof. T. Fujiwara’s contributions to the theoretical and computational study of electronic structures in complex alloys.

Quasicrystals have attracted much interest because they show long-range order without translational periodicity. This unusual atomic structure gives rise to characteristic electronic states and transport properties, which are different from those of ordinary crystals and amorphous alloys. In particular, transition-metal elements play an important role, since their \(d\)-electrons strongly affect the density of states near the Fermi level and can influence electrical conductivity, magnetism, and stability of the quasicrystalline phase.

In this study, we investigate the effect of transition-metal elements on the electronic structure and transport properties of quasicrystals. Special attention is paid to the relation between local atomic environment, hybridization of electronic states, and anomalous transport behavior such as high resistivity and weak temperature dependence. By comparing different transition-metal components, we try to clarify how the electronic structure is modified and how it is connected with observed physical properties.

This work has been carried out in collaboration with Prof. T. Fujiwara, whose theoretical studies on electronic structures of quasicrystals have provided important guidance for the present research. Through this collaboration, we aim to obtain a deeper understanding of the microscopic origin of electronic and transport phenomena in transition-metal-based quasicrystals.
